laager.etymology: D., also leger. Cf. 2d Leaguer, Lair.

label.etymology: OF. label sort of ribbon or fringe, label in heraldry, F. lambeau shred, strip, rag; of uncertain origin; cf. L.labellum, dim. of labrum lip, edge, margin, G. lappen flap, patch, rag, tatter (cf. Lap of a dress), W. llab, llabed, label, flap, Gael. leab, leob, slice, shred, hanging lip.

labial.etymology: LL. labialis, fr. L. labium lip: cf. F. labial. See Lip.

labiate.etymology: NL. labiatus, fr. L. labium lip.

labile.etymology: L. labilis apt to slip, fr. labi to slip.

labor.etymology: OE. labour, OF. labour, laber, labur, F. labeur, L. labor; cf. Gr. labh to get, seize.

laboratory.etymology: Shortened fr. elaboratory; cf. OF. elaboratoire, F. laboratoire. See Elaborate, Labor.

laborious.etymology: L. laboriosus,fr. labor labor: cf. F. laborieux.

labyrinth.etymology: L. labyrinthus, Gr. laby`rinthos: cf. F. labyrinthe.

lac.etymology: Hind. lak, lakh, laksh, Skr. laksha a mark, sign, lakh.

lace.etymology: OE. las, OF. laz, F. lacs, dim. lacet, fr. L. laqueus noose, snare; prob. akin to lacere to entice. Cf. Delight, Elicit, Lasso, Latchet.

lacerate.etymology: L. laceratus, p. p. of lacerare to lacerate, fr. lacer mangled, lacerated; cf. Gr. slay.

lachrymation.etymology: L. lacrimatio, from lacrimare to shed tears, fr. lacrima tear.

lachrymose.etymology: L. lacrymosus, better lacrimosus, fr. lacrima, lacruma (also badly spelt lachryma) a tear, for older dacrima, akin to E. tear. See Tear the secretion.

lack.etymology: OE. lak; cf. D. lak slander, laken to blame, OHG. lahan, AS. leán.

lackey.etymology: F. laquais; cf. Sp. & Pg. lacayo; of uncertain origin; perh. of German origin, and akin to E.lick, v.

lacquer.etymology: F. lacre a sort of sealing wax, Pg. lacte, fr. laca lac. See Lac the resin.

lacrosse.etymology: F. la crosse, lit., the crosier, hooked stick. Cf. Crosier.

lactate.etymology: L. lac, lactis, milk: cf. F. lactate.

lacteal.etymology: L. lacteus milky, fr. lac, lactis, milk. Cf. Galaxy, Lettuce.

lactic.etymology: L. lac, lactis, milk: cf. F. lactique. See Lacteal, and cf. Galactic.

lactifuge.etymology: L. lac, lactis, milk + fugare to expel.

lacuna.etymology: L., ditch, pit, lake, orig., anything hollow. See Lagoon.

lacustrine.etymology: L. lacus lake: cf. F. lacustral, lacustre.

lad.etymology: OE. ladde, of Celtic origin; cf. W. , Ir. lath. (. Cf. Lass.

ladanum.etymology: L. ladanum, ledanum, Fr. (ladan, laden. Cf. Laudanum.

ladder.etymology: OE. laddre, AS. hl, hl; akin to OFries. hladder, OHG.leitara, G. leiter, and from the root of E. lean, v. (Lean, v. i., and cf. Climax.

lade.etymology: AS. hladan to heap, load, draw (water); akin to D. & G. laden to load, OHG. hladan, ladan, Icel. hla, Sw. ladda, Dan. lade, Goth. afhlapan. Cf. Load, Ladle, Lathe for turning, Last a load.

ladin.etymology: From L. Latinus Latin. See Latin

ladle.etymology: AS.hlædel, fr. hladan to load, drain. See Lade, v. t.

lady.etymology: OE. ladi, læfdi, AS. hl, hl; AS. hlaf loaf + a root of uncertain origin, possibly akin to E. dairy. See Loaf, and cf. Lord.

ladybird.etymology: Equiv. to, bird of Our Lady.

lag.etymology: Of Celtic origin: cf. Gael. & Ir. lagweak, feeble, faint, W. llag, llac, slack, loose, remiss, sluggish; prob. akin to E. lax, languid.

roots.meaning: The termination of many English words; as, coward, reynard, drunkard, mostly from the French, in which language this ending is of German origin, being orig. the same word as English hard. It usually has the sense of one who has to a high or excessive degree the quality expressed by the root; as, braggart, sluggard.

lagoon.etymology: It. or Sp. laguna, L. lacuna ditch, pool, pond,lacus lake. See Lake, and cf. Lacuna.

lagophthalmos.etymology: NL. lagophtalmia, fr. Gr. lagw`s hare + 'ofqalmo`s eye; -- so called from the notion that a hare sleeps with his eyes open.

laic.etymology: L. laicus: cf. F. laïque. See Lay laic.

lair.etymology: OE. leir, AS. leger; akin to D. leger, G. lager couch, lair, OHG. laga, Goth. ligrs, and to E. lie. See Lie to be prostrate, and cf. Layer, Leaguer.

lake.etymology: F. laque, fr. Per. See Lac.

lakh.etymology: Hind. lak, lakh, laksh, Skr. laksha a mark, sign, lakh.

lallation.etymology: L. lallare to sing lalla, or lullaby: cf. F. lallation.

lam.etymology: Icel. lemja to beat, or lama to bruise, both fr. lami, lama, lame. See Lame.

lama.etymology: Thibet. blama (pronounced lä''ma) a chief, a high priest.

lamarckism.etymology: From Lamarck, a distinguished French naturalist.

lamb.etymology: AS. lamb; akin to D. & Dan. lam, G. & Sw. lamm, OS., Goth., & Icel. lamb.

lambent.etymology: L. lambens, -enlis, p. pr. of lambere to lick; akin to lap. See Lap to drink by licking.

lame.etymology: OE. lame, AS. lama; akin to D. lam, G. lahm,OHG., Dan., & Sw. lam, Icel. lami, Russ. lomate to break, lomota rheumatism.

lamella.etymology: L. lamella, dim. of lamina plate, leaf, layer: cf. F. lamelle. Cf. Lamina, Omelet.

lamellibranchia.etymology: NL. See lamella, and Branchia, Branchiate.

lament.etymology: F. lamenter, L. lamentari, fr. lamentum a lament.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

lammas.etymology: AS. hlammesse, hlafmæsse, loaf mass, bread feast, or feast of first fruits; hlaf loaf + mæsse mass. See Loaf, and Mass religious service.

lammergeier.etymology: G. lämmergeier; lamm, pl. lämmer, lamb + geier vulture.

lamp.etymology: OE. (with excrescent p), fr. F. lame, L. lamina. See Lamina.

lampoon.etymology: F. lampon a drinking song, fr. lampons let us drink, -- the burden of such a song, fr. lamper to guzzle, to drink much and greedily; of German origin, and akin to E. lap to drink. Prob. so called because drinking songs often contain personal slander or satire.

lamprey.etymology: OE. lampreie, F. lamproie, LL. lampreda, lampetra, from L. lambere to lick + petra rock, stone. The lampreys are so called because they attach themselves with their circular mouths to rocks and stones, whence they are also called rocksuckers. See Lap to drink, Petrify.

lanate.etymology: L. lanatus, fr. lana wool, down.

lance.etymology: OE. lance, F. lance, fr. L. lancea; cf. Gr. Launch.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix having a diminutive force; as in streamlet, armlet.

lanceolate.etymology: L. lanceolatus: cf. F. lancéol. See Lanceolar.

lancet.etymology: F. lancette, dim. of lance lance. See Lance.

lancinate.etymology: L. lancinatus, p. p. of lancinare to fear.

land.etymology: AS. land, lond; akin to D., G., Icel., Sw., Dan., and Goth. land.

landau.etymology: From the town Ladau in Germany; cf. F. landau. See Land, Island.

landgrave.etymology: G. landgraf; land land + graf earl, count; cf. D. landgraaf, F. landgrave.

landlubber.etymology: Prop. fr. land + lubber, or possibly corrupted fr. laudlouper.

landmark.etymology: AS. landmearc. See Land, and Mark a sign.

landscape.etymology: D. landschap; land land + -schap, equiv. to E. -schip; akin to G. landschaft, Sw. landskap, Dan. landskab. See Land, and -schip.

language.etymology: OE. langage, F. langage, fr. L. lingua the tongue, hence speech, language; akin to E. tongue. See Tongue, cf. Lingual.

languid.etymology: L. languidus, fr. languere to be faint or languid: cf. F. languide. See Languish.

languish.etymology: OE. languishen, languissen, F. languir, L. languere; cf. Gr. lakra to lag behind; prob. akin to E. lag, lax, and perh. to E. slack.See -ish.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

languor.etymology: OE. langour, OF. langour, F. langueur, L. languor. See Languish.

laniary.etymology: L. laniarius, fr. lanius butcher, laniare to tear in pieces: cf. F. laniaire.

lank.etymology: AS. hlanc; cf. G. lenken to turn, gelenk joint, OHG. hlanca hip, side, flank, and E. link of a chain.

lantern.etymology: F. lanterne, L. lanterna, laterna, from Gr. Lamp.

lanyard.etymology: F.lanière thong, strap, OF. lasniere, fr. lasne strap, thong, L. lacinia lappet. flap, edge of a garment. Cf. Lanier.

lap.etymology: OE. lappe, AS. læppa; akin to D. lap patch, piece, G. lappen, OHG. lappa, Dan. lap, Sw. lapp.

lapidary.etymology: L. lapidarius, fr. lapidarius pertaining to stone: cf. F. lapidaire.

lapidate.etymology: L.lapidatus, p. p. of lapidare, fr. lapis stone.

lapidify.etymology: Cf. f. lapidifier. See Lapidific, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

lapse.etymology: L. lapsus, fr. labi, p. p. lapsus, to slide, to fall: cf. F. laps. See Sleep.

lapwing.etymology: OE.lapwynke, leepwynke, AS. hleápewince; hleápan to leap, jump + (prob.) a word akin to AS. wincian to wink, E. wink, AS. wancol wavering; cf. G. wanken to stagger, waver. See Leap, and Wink.

larboard.etymology: Lar- is of uncertain origin, possibly the same as lower, i. e., humbler in rank, because the starboard side is considered by mariners as higher in rank; cf. D. laag low, akin to E. low. See Board, n., 8.

larceny.etymology: F. larcin, OE. larrecin, L. latrocinium, fr. latro robber, mercenary, hired servant; cf. Gr. (Latrociny.

large.etymology: F., fr. L. largus. Cf. Largo.

largess.etymology: F. largesse, fr. large. See Large, a.

largesse.etymology: F. largesse, fr. large. See Large, a.

largo.etymology: It., large, L. largus, See Large.

lariat.etymology: Sp. la reata the rope; la the + reata rope. Cf. Reata.

lark.etymology: Perh fr. AS. lac play, sport. Cf. Lake, v. i.

larrup.etymology: Perh, a corrupt. of lee rope, used by sailors in beating the boys; but cf. D. larpen to thresh, larp a whip, blow.

roots.meaning: A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

lascar.etymology: Per. & Hind. lashkar an army, an inferior artillery man, a cooly, a native sailor.

lascivious.etymology: L. lascivia wantonness, fr. lascivus wanton; cf. Gr. (lash to desire.

lash.etymology: OE. lasche; cf. D. lasch piece set in, joint, seam, G. lashe latchet, a bit of leather, gusset, stripe, laschen to furnish with flaps, to lash or slap, Icel. laski gusset, flap, laska to break.

lass.etymology: OE. lasse; prob. of Celtic origin; cf. W. llodes girl, fem. of llawd lad. (Lad a youth.

lassitude.etymology: L. lassitudo, fr. lassus faint, weary; akin to E. late: cf. F. lassitude. See Late.

lasso.etymology: Sp. lazo, L. laqueus. See Lace.

last.etymology: OE. last, latst, contr. of latest, superl. of late; akin to OS. lezt, lazt, last, D. laatst, G. letzt. See Late, and cf. Latest.

latch.etymology: Cf. F. lécher to lick (of German origin). Cf. Lick.

latchet.etymology: OE. lachet, from an OF. dialect form of F. lacet plaited string, lace dim. of lacs. See Lace.

late.etymology: OE. lat slow, slack, As.læt; akin to Os. lat, D. laat late, G. lass weary, lazy, slack, Icel. latr, Sw. lat, Dan. lad, Goth. lats, and to E. let, v. See Let to permit, and cf. Alas, Lassitude.

latent.etymology: L. latens, -entis, p. pr. of latere to lie hid or concealed; cf. Gr. lethargy: cf. F.latent.

lateral.etymology: L. lateralis, fr. latus, lateris, side: cf. F.latéral.

laterite.etymology: L. later brick, tile: cf. F. latérite.

lath.etymology: OE. laththe, latthe, latte, AS. lætta; akin to D. lat, G. latte, OHG. latta; cf. W. llath a rod, staff, yard. Cf. Lattice, Latten.

lather.etymology: AS. leáedhor niter, in leáedhorwyrt soapwort; cf. Icel. lau; perh. akin to E. lye.

latin.etymology: F., fr. L. Latinus belonging to Latium, Latin, fr. Latium a country of Italy, in which Rome was situated. Cf. Ladin, Lateen sail, under Lateen.

latitude.etymology: F. latitude, L. latitudo, fr. latus broad, wide, for older stlatus; perh. akin to E. strew.

latten.etymology: OE. latoun, laton, OF. laton, F. laiton, prob. fr. OF. late lath, F. latte; -- because made in thin plates; cf. It. latta a sheet of tinned iron, tin plate. F. latte is of German origin. See Lath a thin board.

latter.etymology: OE. later, lætter, compar. of lat late. See Late, and cf. Later.

lattice.etymology: OE. latis, F. lattis lathwork, fr. latte lath. See Latten, 1st Lath.

laud.etymology: L. laus, laudis. See Laud, v. i.

laudable.etymology: L. laudabilis: cf. OE. laudable. See Laud, v. i.

laudanum.etymology: Orig. the same wort as ladanum, ladbdanum: cf. F. laudanum, It. laudano, ladano. See Ladanum.

laugh.etymology: OE. laughen, laghen, lauhen, AS. hlehhan, hlihhan, hlyhhan, hliehhan; akin to OS. hlahan, D. & G.lachen, OHG. hlahhan, lahhan, lahh, Icel. hlæja. Dan. lee, Sw. le, Goth. hlahjan; perh. of imitative origin.

laughter.etymology: AS. hleahtor; akin to OHG. hlahtar, G. gelächter, Icel. hlatr, Dan. latter. See Laugh, v. i.

launce.etymology: It. lance, L. lanx, lancis, plate, scale of a balance. Cf. Balance.

launch.etymology: OE. launchen to throw as a lance, OF. lanchier, another form of lancier, F. lancer, fr. lance lance. See Lance.

launder.etymology: Contracted fr. OE. lavender, F. lavandière, LL. lavandena, from L. lavare to wash. See Lave.

laundry.etymology: OE. lavendrie, OF. lavanderie. See Launder.

laureate.etymology: L. laureatus, fr. laurea laurel tree, fr. laureus of laurel, fr. laurus laurel: cf. F. lauréat. Cf. Laurel.

laurel.etymology: OE. lorel, laurer, lorer, OF. lorier, laurier, F. laurier, (assumed) LL. Laurarius, fr. L. laurus.

lava.etymology: It. lava lava, orig. in Naples, a torrent of rain overflowing the streets, fr. It. & L. lavare to wash. See Lave.

lavatory.etymology: L. lavatorium: cf. lavatoire. See Lave to wash, and cf. Laver.

lave.etymology: F. laver, L. lavare, akin to luere to wash, Gr. Ablution, Deluge, Lavender, Lava, Lotion.

lavender.etymology: OE. lavendre, F. lavande, It. lavanda lavender, a washing, fr. L. lavare to wash; cf. It. lsavendola, LL. lavendula. So called because it was used in bathing and washing. See Lave. to wash, and cf. Lavender.

laver.etymology: OE. lavour, F. lavoir, L. lavatorium a washing place. See Lavatory.

lavish.etymology: Akin to E. lave to lade out; cf. AS. gelafian to refresh, G. laben.

law.etymology: OE. lawe, laghe, AS. lagu, from the root of E. lie: akin to OS. lag, Icel. lög, Sw. lag, Dan. lov; cf. L. lex, E. legal. A law is that which is laid, set, or fixed; like statute, fr. L. statuere to make to stand. See Lie to be prostrate.

lawn.etymology: OE. laund, launde, F. lande heath, moor; of Celtic origin; cf. W. llan an open, clear place, llawnt a smooth rising hill, lawn, Armor. lann or lan territory, country, lann a prickly plant, pl. lannou heath, moor.

lax.etymology: L. laxus Cf. Laches, Languish, Lease, v. t., Leash.

laxation.etymology: L. laxatio, fr. laxare to loosen, fr. laxus loose, slack.

laxative.etymology: L. laxativus mitigating, assuaging: cf. F. laxatif. See Lax, a.

laxity.etymology: L. laxitas, fr. laxus loose, slack: cf. F. laxité, See Lax, a.

lay.etymology: F. lai, L. laicus, Gr. Laic.

layer.etymology: See Lay to cause to lie flat.

lazar.etymology: OF. lazare, fr. Lazarus the beggar. Luke xvi. 20.

lazaret.etymology: F. lazaret, or It. lazzeretto, fr. Lazarus. See Lazar.

lazaretto.etymology: F. lazaret, or It. lazzeretto, fr. Lazarus. See Lazar.

lazuli.etymology: F. & NL. lapis lazuli, LL. lazulus, lazurius, lazur from the same Oriental source as E. azure. See Azure.

lazy.etymology: OE. lasie, laesic, of uncertain origin; cf. F. las tired, L. lassus, akin to E. late; or cf. LG. losig, lesig.

lea.etymology: Cf. Lay, n. (that which is laid), 4.

leach.etymology: Cf. As. leáh lye, G. lauge. See Lye.

lead.etymology: OE. led, leed, lead, AS. leád; akin to D. lood, MHG. lot, G. loth plummet, sounding lead, small weight, Sw. & Dan. lod. sq. root123

leaf.etymology: OE. leef, lef, leaf, AS. leáf; akin to S. l, OFries. laf, D. loof foliage, G. laub,OHG. loub leaf, foliage, Icel. lauf, Sw. löf, Dan. löv, Goth. laufs; cf. Lith. lapas. Cf. Lodge.

league.etymology: Cf. OE. legue, lieue, a measure of length, F. lieue, Pr. lega, legua, It. & LL. lega, Sp. legua, Pg. legoa, legua; all fr. LL. leuca, of Celtic origin: cf. Arm. leo, lev (perh. from French), Ir.leige (perh. from English); also Ir. & Gael. leac a flag, a broad, flat stone, W. llech, -- such stones having perh. served as a sort of milestone (cf. Cromlech).

leak.etymology: Akin to D. lek leaky, a leak, G.leck, Icel. lekr leaky, Dan. læk leaky, a leak, Sw. läck; cf. AS. hlec full of cracks or leaky. Cf. Leak, v.

leal.etymology: OE. leial, another form of loial, F. loyal. See Loyal.

lean.etymology: Icel. leyna; akin to G. läugnen to deny, AS. l, also E. lie to speak falsely.

learn.etymology: OE. lernen, leornen, AS. leornian; akin to OS. linon, for lirnon, OHG. lirnen, lernen, G. lernen, fr. the root of AS. l to teach, OS. lerian, OHG.leran, G. lehren, Goth. laisjan, also Goth lais I know, leis acquainted (in comp.); all prob. from a root meaning, to go, go over, and hence, to learn; cf. AS. leoran to go . Cf. Last a mold of the foot, lore.

lease.etymology: AS. lesan to gather; akin to D. lezen to gather, read, G. lesen, Goth. lisan to gather; cf. Lith lesti to peck.

leash.etymology: OE. lese, lees, leece, OF. lesse, F. laisse, LL.laxa, fr. L. laxus loose. See Lax.

least.etymology: OE. last, lest, AS. l, l, superl. of l less. See Less, a.

leather.etymology: OE. lether, AS. le; akin to D. leder, leêr, G. leder, OHG. ledar, Icel. le, Sw. läder, Dan. læder.

leaven.etymology: OE. levain, levein, F. levain, L. levamen alleviation, mitigation; but taken in the sense of, a raising, that which raises, fr. levare to raise. See Lever, n.

lecher.etymology: OE.lechur, lechour, OF.lecheor, lecheur, gormand, glutton, libertine, parasite, fr. lechier to lick, F. lécher; of Teutonic origin. See Lick.

lechery.etymology: OE. lecherie, OF. lecherie. See Lecher.

lecture.etymology: F. lecture, LL. lectura, fr. L. legere, lectum, to read. See Legend.

ledge.etymology: Akin to AS. licgan to lie, Icel. liggja; cf. Icel. lögg the ledge or rim at the bottom of a cask. See Lie to be prostrate.

ledger.etymology: Akin to D. legger layer, daybook (fr. leggen to lay, liggen to lie), E. ledge, lie. See Lie to be prostrate.

lee.etymology: F. lie, perh. fr. L. levare to lift up, raise. Cf. Lever.

leech.etymology: Cf. LG. leik, Icel. lik, Sw. lik boltrope, stliken the leeches.

leek.etymology: AS.leác; akin to D. look, G. lauch, OHG. louh, Icel. laukr, Sw. lök, Dan lög. Cf. Garlic.

leer.etymology: OE. lere; akin to G. leer, OHG. & OS. lari.

left.etymology: OE. left, lift, luft; akin to Fries. leeft, OD.lucht, luft; cf. AS.left (equiv. to L. inanis), lyftadl palsy; or cf. AS.l weak.

leg.etymology: Icel. leggr; akin to Dan. læg calf of the leg, Sw. lägg.

legacy.etymology: L. (assumed) legatia, for legatum, from legare to appoint by last will, to bequeath as a legacy, to depute: cf. OF. legat legacy. See Legate.

legal.etymology: L. legalis, fr. lex, legis, law; prob. orig., that which lies or is fixed (cf. L. lectus bed), and if so akin to E. lie, law: cf. F. légal. Cf. Lie to be prostrate, Loyal, Leal.

legality.etymology: Cf. LL. legalitas, F. légalité. Cf. Loyalty.

legate.etymology: OE. legal, L. legatus, fr. legare to sent with a commission or charge, to depute, fr. lex, legis, law: cf. F. légat, It. legato. See Legal.

legation.etymology: L. legatio: cf. F. légation, It. legazione. See Legate.

legato.etymology: It., tied, joined, fr. legare to tie, bind, L. ligare.

legend.etymology: OE. legende, OF. legende, F. légende, LL. legenda, fr. L. legendus to be read, fr. legere to read, gather; akin to Gr. Collect, Dialogue, Lesson, Logic.

legerdemain.etymology: F. léger light, nimble + de of + main hand, L. manus. See 3d Leger, and Manual.

legible.etymology: L. legibilis, fr. legere to read: cf. OF. legible. See Legend.

legion.etymology: OE. legioun, OF. legion, F. légion, fr. L. legio, fr. legere to gather, collect. See Legend.

legislation.etymology: Cf. F. législation, L. legis latio. See Legislator.

legislator.etymology: L. legis lator, prop., a proposer of a law; lex, legis, law + lator a proposer, bearer, fr. latus, used as p. p. of ferre to bear: cf. F. législateur. See Legal, and Tolerate.

legitimate.etymology: LL. legitimatus, p. p. of legitimare to legitimate, fr. L. legitimus legitimate. See Legal.

legume.etymology: F. légume, L. legumen, fr. legere to gather. So called because they may be gathered without cutting. See Legend.

leisure.etymology: OE. leisere, leiser, OF.leisir, F. loisir, orig., permission, fr. L. licere to be permitted. See License.

lemming.etymology: Nor. lemming, lemende; cf. Sw. lemel, Lapp. lummik.

lemon.etymology: F. limon, Per. lim; cf. Ar.laim, Sp. limon, It. limone. Cf. Lime a fruit.

lemonade.etymology: F. limonade; cf. Sp. limonada, It. limonata. See Lemon.

lemur.etymology: L., a ghost, specter. So called on account of its habit of going abroad by night.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

lend.etymology: OE.lenen, AS. l, fr. l loan; akin to G. lehnen to lend. See Loan.

length.etymology: OE. lengthe, AS. leng, fr. land, long, long; akin to D. lengte, Dan. længde, Sw. längd, Icel. lengd. See Long, a.

lenient.etymology: L. leniens, -entis, p. pr. of lenire to soften, fr. lenis soft, mild. Cf. Lithe.

lenify.etymology: L. lenis soft, mild + -fy: cf. F.lénifier.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

lenity.etymology: L. lenitas, fr. lenis soft, mild: cf. OF. lenité. See Lenient.

lens.etymology: L. lens a lentil. So named from the resemblance in shape of a double convex lens to the seed of a lentil. Cf. Lentil.

lent.etymology: OE. lente, lenten, leynte, AS. lengten, lencten, spring, lent, akin to D. lente, OHG. lenzin, langiz, G. lenz, and perh. fr. AS. lang long, E. long, because at this season of the year the days lengthen.

lenten.etymology: From OE. lenten lent. See Lent, n.

lenticel.etymology: F. lenticelle, dim. fr. L. lens, lentis, a lentil. Cf. Lentil.

lenticular.etymology: L. lenticularis: cf. F. lenticulaire. See Lenticel.

lentiform.etymology: L. lens, lentis, lentil + -form: cf. F. lentifarme,

lentil.etymology: F. lentille, fr. L. lenticula, dim. of lens, lentis, lentil. Cf. Lens.

lentisk.etymology: L. lentiscus, lentiscum: cf. F. lentisque.

leonine.etymology: L. leoninus, fr. leo, leonis, lion: cf. F. léonin. See Lion.

leopard.etymology: OE. leopart, leparde, lebarde, libbard, OF. leopard, liepart, F. léopard, L. leopardus, fr. Gr. Lion, and Pard.

roots.meaning: Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.

leprous.etymology: OF. leprous, lepros, F. lépreux, fr. L. leprosus, fr. lepra, leprae, leprosy. See Leper.

lesion.etymology: F. lesion, L. laesio, fr. laedere, laesum, to hurt, injure.

less.etymology: OE. lesse, AS. læssa; akin to OFries. lessa; a compar. from a lost positive form. Cf. Lesser, Lest, Least. Less has the sense of the comparative degree of little.

lessee.etymology: F. laissé, p. p. of laisser. See Lease, v. t.

lesser.etymology: This word is formed by adding anew the compar. suffix -er (in which r is from an original s) to less. See Less, a.

lesson.etymology: OE. lessoun, F. le lesson, reading, fr. L. lectio a reading, fr. legere to read, collect. See Legend, and cf. Lection.

let.etymology: OE.letten, AS. lettan to delay, to hinder, fr. læt slow; akin to D. letten to hinder, G. verletzen to hurt, Icel. letja to hold back, Goth. latjan. See Late.

lethargic.etymology: L. lethargicus, Gr. léthargique. See Lethargy.

lethargy.etymology: F. léthargie, L. letgargia, Gr. Lethe.

lettuce.etymology: OE. letuce, prob. through Old French from some Late Latin derivative of L. lactuca lettuce, which, according to Varro, is fr. lac, lactis, milk, on account of the milky white juice which flows from it when it is cut: cf. F. laitue. Cf. Lacteal, Lactucic.

levant.etymology: F., p. pr. of lever to raise.

levantine.etymology: F. levantin, or It. levantino. See Levant, n.

levator.etymology: NL., fr. L. levare to raise. See Lever, n.

levee.etymology: F. lever, fr. lever to raise, se lever to rise. See Lever, n.

level.etymology: OE. level, livel, OF. livel, F. niveau, fr. L. libella level, water level, a plumb level, dim. of libra pound, measure for liquids, balance, water poise, level. Cf. Librate, Libella.

lever.etymology: Old compar. of leve or lief.

leveret.etymology: F. levraut, dim. of lièvre hare, L. lepus. Cf. Leporine.

levirate.etymology: L. levir a husband's brother, brother-in-law; akin to Gr. lévirat leviration.

levite.etymology: L. Levites, Gr. Levi, one of the sons of Jacob.

levity.etymology: L. levitas, fr. levis light in weight; akin to levare to raise. See Lever, n.

roots.meaning: A prefix from L. laevus, meaning: (a) Pertaining to, or toward, the left; as, levorotatory. (b) (Chem. & Opt.) Turning the plane of polarized light to the left; as, levotartaric acid; levoracemic acid; levogyratory crystals, etc. [Written also lævo-.]

A prefix from L. laevus, meaning: (a) Pertaining to, or toward, the left; as, levorotatory. (b) (Chem. & Opt.) Turning the plane of polarized light to the left; as, levotartaric acid; levoracemic acid; levogyratory crystals, etc. [Written also lævo-.]

levy.etymology: A contr. of elevenpence or elevenpenny bit.

lewd.etymology: OE.lewed, lewd, lay, ignorant, vile, AS. l laical, belonging to the laity.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

liable.etymology: From F. lier to bind, L. ligare. Cf. Ally, v. t., Ligature.

liaison.etymology: Borrowed from French liaison ( “ binding ” ) , from Latin ligātiō (stem ligātiōn- ; whence the English doublet ligation ), derived from ligō ( “ to bind ” ) , from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- ( “ to bind ” ) .

liana.etymology: F. liane; prob. akin to lien a band, fr. L. ligamen, fr. ligare to bind. Cf. Lien, n.

liar.etymology: OE. liere. See Lie to falsify.

libation.etymology: L. libatio, fr. libare to take a little from anything, to taste, to pour out as an offering: cf. F. libation.

libel.etymology: L. libellus a little book, pamphlet, libel, lampoon, dim. of liber the liber or inner bark of a tree; also (because the ancients wrote on this bark), paper, parchment, or a roll of any material used to write upon, and hence, a book or treatise: cf. F. libelle.

liberal.etymology: F. libéral, L. liberalis, from liber free; perh. akin to libet, lubet,it pleases, E. lief. Cf. Deliver.

liberate.etymology: L. liberatus, p. p. of liberare to free, fr. liber free. See Liberal, a., and cf. Deliver.

liberation.etymology: L. liberatio: cf. F. libération. Cf. Livraison.

libertine.etymology: L. libertinus freedman, from libertus one made free, fr. liber free: cf. F. libertin. See Liberal.

liberty.etymology: OE. liberte, F. liberté, fr. L. libertas, fr. liber free. See Liberal.

libidinous.etymology: L. libidinosus, fr. libido, libidinis, pleasure, desire, lust, fr. libet, lubet, it pleases: cf. F. libidineux. See Lief.

library.etymology: From Middle English librarie , from Anglo-Norman librarie , from Old French librairie , from Latin librarium ( “ bookcase, chest for books ” ) , from librarius ( “ concerning books ” ) , from liber ( “ the inner bark of trees; paper, parchment, book ” ) , probably derived from a Proto-Indo-European base *leub(ʰ)- ( “ to strip, to peel ” ) . Displaced native Middle English bochous, bokhus ( literally “ book house ” ) , from Old English bōchūs (compare bookhouse ).

librate.etymology: L. libratus, p. p. of librare to balance, to make even, fr. libra.Cf. Level, Deliberate, Equilibrium.

libretto.etymology: It., dim. of libro book, L. liber. See Libel.

license.etymology: F. licence, L. licentia, fr. licere to be permitted, prob. orig., to be left free to one; akin to linquere to leave. See Loan, and cf. Illicit, Leisure.

licentiate.etymology: LL. licentiatus, fr. licentiare to allow to do anything, fr. L. licentia license. See License, n.

licentious.etymology: L. licentiosus: cf. F. licencieux. See License.

licit.etymology: L.licitus permitted, lawful, from licere: cf. F. licite. See License.

lick.etymology: AS. liccian; akin to OS. likk, D. likken, OHG. lecch, G. lecken, Goth. bi-laig, Russ. lizate, L. lingere, Gr. lih, rih. . Cf. Lecher, Relish.

licorice.etymology: OE. licoris, though old French, fr. L. liquiritia, corrupted fr. glycyrrhiza, Gr. Glycerin, Glycyrrhiza, Wort.

lie.etymology: AS. lyge; akin to D. leugen, OHG. lugi, G. lüge, lug, Icel. lygi, Dan. & Sw. lögn, Goth. liugn. See Lie to utter a falsehood.

lief.etymology: OE. leef, lef, leof, AS. leóf; akin to OS.liof, OFries. liaf, D. lief, G. lieb, OHG. liob, Icel. lj, Sw.ljuf, Goth. liubs, and E. love. sq. root124. See Love, and cf. Believe, Leave, n., Furlough, Libidinous.

liege.etymology: OE. lige, lege, F. lige, LL. ligius, legius, liege, unlimited, complete, prob. of German origin; cf. G. ledig free from bonds and obstacles, MHG. ledec, ledic, lidic, freed, loosed, and Charta Ottonis de Benthem, ann. ligius homo quod Teutonicè dicitur ledigman," i. e., uni soli homagio obligatus, free from all obligations to others; influenced by L.ligare to bind. G. ledig perh. orig. meant, free to go where one pleases, and is perh. akin to E.lead to conduct. Cf. Lead to guide.

lien.etymology: F. lien band, bond, tie, fr. L. ligamen, fr. ligare to bind. Cf. League a union, Leam a string, Leamer, Ligament.

lieu.etymology: F., OF. also liu, leu, lou, fr. L. locus place. See Local, Locus.

lieutenant.etymology: F., fr. lieu place + tenant holding, p. pr. of tenir to hold, L. tenere. See Lieu, and Tenant, and cf. Locum tenens.

life.etymology: AS. l; akin to D. lijf body, G. leib body, MHG. l life, body, OHG. l life, Icel. l, life, body, Sw. lif, Dan. liv, and E. live, v. Live, and cf. Alive.

ligament.etymology: L. ligamentum, fr. ligare to bind; cf. f. ligament. Cf. Lien, n., Ligature.

ligan.etymology: Cf. L. ligare to bind, to tie, ligamen band, bandage, E. ligament, or ligsam.

ligate.etymology: L. ligatus, p. p. of ligare.

ligation.etymology: L. ligatio, fr. ligare to bind. Cf. Liaison.

ligature.etymology: L. ligatura, fr. ligare, ligatum, to bind: cf. f. ligature. Cf. Ally, League, Legatura, Liable, Legament.

light.etymology: OE.light, liht, AS. leót; akin to OS. lioht, D. & G. licht, OHG. lioht, Goth. liuhap, Icel. lj, L. lux light, lucere to shine, Gr. ruc to shine. Lucid, Lunar, Luminous, Lynx.

lighter.etymology: D. ligter, fr. ligt light. See Light not heavy.

lightning.etymology: For lightening, fr. lighten to flash.

ligneous.etymology: L. ligneus, fr. lignum wood. Cf. Lignous.

lignify.etymology: L. lignum wood + -fy: cf. F. lignifier.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

lignin.etymology: L. lignum wood: cf. F. lignine.

lignite.etymology: L. lignum wood: cf. F. lignite.

ligule.etymology: L.ligula, little tongue, dim of lingua tongue : cf. F. ligule.

like.etymology: OE. lik, ilik, gelic, AS. gelic, fr. pref. ge- + lic body, and orig. meaning, having the same body, shape, or appearance, and hence, like; akin to OS. gilik, D. gelijk, G. gleich, OHG. gilih, Icel. likr, glikr, Dan. lig, Sw. lik, Goth. galeiks, OS. lik body, D. lijk, G. leiche, Icel. lik, Sw. lik, Goth. leik. The English adverbial ending-ly is from the same adjective. Cf. Each, Such, Which.

roots.meaning: An Anglo-Saxon prefix. See Y-.
A termination denoting state, condition, quality, character, totality, as in manhood, childhood, knighthood, brotherhood. Sometimes it is written, chiefly in obsolete words, in the form - head.

likely.etymology: That is, like-like. See Like, a.

lilac.etymology: Sp. lilac, lila, Ar.lilak, fr. Per. lilaj, lilanj, lilang, nilaj, nil, the indigo plant, or from the kindred lilak bluish, the flowers being named from the color. Cf. Anil.

liliaceous.etymology: L. liliaceus, fr. lilium lily. See Lily.

lilt.etymology: Cf. Norw. lilla, lirla, to sing in a high tone.

lily.etymology: AS. lilie, L. lilium, Gr. Flower-de- luce.

roots.meaning: A prefix from Latin de down, from, away; as in debark, decline, decease, deduct, decamp. In words from the French it is equivalent to Latin dis- apart, away; or sometimes to de. Cf. Dis-. It is negative and opposite in derange, deform, destroy, etc. It is intensive in deprave, despoil, declare, desolate, etc.

liman.etymology: F. limon, fr. L. limus slime.

limb.etymology: OE. lim, AS. lim; akin to Icel. limr limb, lim branch of a tree, Sw. & Dan. lem limb; cf. also AS. li, OHG. lid, gilid, G. glied, Goth. lipus. Cf. Lith, Limber.

limber.etymology: For limmer, Icel. limar branches, boughs, pl. of lim; akin to E. limb. See Limb a branch.

limbo.etymology: L. limbus border, edge in limbo on the border. Cf. Limb border.

limbus.etymology: L. limbus border, edge in limbo on the border. Cf. Limb border.

limicolae.etymology: L. limicola a dweller in the mud; limus mud + colere to dwell.

limit.etymology: From L. limes, limitis: cf. F.limite; -or from E. limit, v. See Limit, v. t.

limitation.etymology: L. limitatio: cf. F. Limitation. See Limit, v. t.

limn.etymology: OE. limnen, fr. luminen, for enluminen, F. enluminer to illuminate, to limn, LL. illuminare to paint. Illuminate, Luminous.

limner.etymology: F. enlumineur, LL. illuminator. See Limn, and cf. Alluminor.

limp.etymology: Cf. Icel. limpa limpness, weakness, and E.lap, n., lop, v. t. Cf. Limber, a.

limpid.etymology: L.limpidus; akin to Gr. limpide. Cf. Lamp.

limulus.etymology: L., dim. of limus sidelong, askance.

linchpin.etymology: AS. lynis the axletree; akin to D. luns linchpin, OS. lunisa, LG. lunse, G. lünse, OHG. lun peg, bolt.

linden.etymology: Orig. an adj. from lind linden tree, AS. lind; akin to D. & G. linde, OHG. linta, Icel., Sw., & Dan. lind. Cf. Lime linden.

lineage.etymology: OE. linage, F. lignage, fr. L. linea line. See 3d Line.

lineal.etymology: L. linealis belonging to a line, fr. linea line: cf. F. linéal. See 3d Line.

lineament.etymology: L. lineamentum, fr. linea line: cf. F. linéament. See 3d Line.

linear.etymology: L. linearis, linearius , fr. linea line: cf. F. linéaire. See 3d Line.

lineation.etymology: L. lineatio the drawing of a line, fr. lineare.

linen.etymology: Prop. an adj. from OE. lin. flax, AS. lin flax, whence linen made of flax; akin to OS., Icel., & MHG. lin flax and linen, G. lein, leinen, linen, Sw. lin flax, Goth. lein linen, L. linum flax, linen, Gr. Line, Linseed.

ling.etymology: OE. lenge; akin to D. leng, G. länge, Dan. lange, Sw. l, Icel. langa. So named from its being long. See Long, a.

linger.etymology: OE. lengen to tarry, AS. lengan to prolong, put off, fr. lang long. Long, a.

lingo.etymology: L. lingua tongue, language. See Lingual.

lingual.etymology: L. lingua tongue: cf. F. lingual. See Tongue, and cf. Language.

linguist.etymology: L. lingua tongue, speech, language: cf. F. linguiste.

lingulate.etymology: L. lingulatus, fr. lingula a little tongue. Cf. Ligulate.

liniment.etymology: L. linimentum, fr. linire, linere, to besmear, anoint : cf. F. liniment. Cf. Letter, Lime a viscous substance.

lining.etymology: See Line to cover the in side.

link.etymology: Prob. corrupted from lint and this for lunt a torch, match, D. lont match; akin to G. lunte, cf. MHG. lünden to burn. Cf. Lunt, Linstock.

linnet.etymology: F. linot, linotte, from L. linum flax; or perh. shortened from AS.linetwige, fr. AS. lin flax; -- so called because it feeds on the seeds of flax and hemp. See Linen.

linseed.etymology: OE. lin flax + seed. See Linen.

linstock.etymology: Corrupt. fr. luntstock, D. lonistok; lont lunt + stok stock, stick. See Link a torch, Lunt, and Stock.

lint.etymology: AS. linet flax, hemp, fr. lin flax; or, perh. borrowed fr. L. linteum a linen cloth, linen, from linteus linen, a., fr. lineum flax, lint. See Linen.

lintel.etymology: OE. lintel, F. linteau, LL. lintellus, for limitellus, a dim. fr. L. limes limit. See Limit.

lion.etymology: F. lion, L. leo, -onis, akin to Gr. Chameleon, Dandelion, Leopard.

lip.etymology: OE. lippe, AS. lippa; akin to D. lip, G. lippe, lefze, OHG. lefs, Dan. læbe, Sw. läpp, L. labium, labrum. Cf. Labial.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.

liquefaction.etymology: L. liquefactio: cf. F. liquéfaction. See Liquefy.

liquefy.etymology: F. liquéfier, L. liquere to be liquid + facere, - ficare (in comp.), to make. See Liquid, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

liquescent.etymology: L. liquescens, p. pr. of liquescere to become liquid, incho. fr. liquere to be liquid.

liquid.etymology: L. liquidus, fr. liquere to be fluid or liquid; cf. Skr. ri to ooze, drop, li to melt.

liquidate.etymology: LL. liquidatus, p. p. of liquidate to liquidate, fr. L. liquidus liquid, clear. See Liquid.

liquidity.etymology: L. liquiditas, fr. liquidus liquid: cf. F. liquidité.

liquor.etymology: OE. licour, licur, OF. licur, F. liqueur, fr. L. liquor, fr. liquere to be liquid. See Liquid, and cf. Liqueur.

lira.etymology: It., fr. L. libra the Roman pound. Cf. Livre.

lisp.etymology: OE. lispen, lipsen, AS. wlisp stammering, lisping; akin to D. & OHG. lispen to lisp, G. lispeln, Sw. läspa, Dan. lespe.

list.etymology: F. lice, LL. liciae, pl., from L. licium thread, girdle.

listen.etymology: OE. listnen, listen, lustnen, lusten, AS. hlystan; akin to hlyst hearing, OS. hlust, Icel. hlusta to listen, hlust ear, AS. hlosnian to wait in suspense, OHG. hlosen to listen, Gr. loud. sq. root41. See Loud, and cf. List to listen.

literal.etymology: F. litéral, littéral, L. litteralis, literalis, fr. littera, litera, a letter. See Letter.

literary.etymology: L. litterarius, literarius,fr. littera, litera, a letter: cf. F. littéraire. See Letter.

literature.etymology: F. littérature, L. litteratura, literatura, learning, grammar, writing, fr.littera, litera, letter. See Letter.

lithesome.etymology: See Lithe, a., and cf. Lissom.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
A combining form denoting divination; as, aleuromancy, chiromancy, necromancy, etc.

litigant.etymology: L. litigans, -antis, p. pr. of litigare: cf. F. litigant. See Litigate.

litigation.etymology: L. litigatio, fr. litigare to dispute, litigate; lis, litis, dispute, lawsuit (OL. stlis) + agere to carry on. See Agent.

litigious.etymology: L. litigiosus, fr. litigium dispute, quarrel, fr. litigare: cf. F. litigieux. See Litigation.

litmus.etymology: D. lakmoes; lak lacker + moes a thick preparation of fruit, pap, prob. akin to E. meat: cf. G. lackmus. See Lac a resinous substance.

litter.etymology: F. litière, LL. lectaria, fr. L. lectus couch, bed. See Lie to be prostrated, and cf. Coverlet.

little.etymology: OE. litel, lutel, AS. l, litel, l; akin to OS. littil, D. luttel, LG. lütt, OHG. luzzil, MHG. lützel; and perh. to AS. lytig deceitful, lot deceit, Goth. liuts deceitful, lut to deceive; cf. also Icel. litill little, Sw. liten, Dan. liden, lille, Goth. leitils, which appear to have a different root vowel.

littoral.etymology: L. littoralis, litoralis, from littus, litus, the seashore: cf. F. littoral.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

liturgy.etymology: F. liturgie, LL. liturgia, Gr. Lay, a., and Work.

live.etymology: OE. liven, livien, AS. libban, lifian; akin to OS. libbian, D. leven, G. leben, OHG. lebn, Dan. leve, Sw. lefva, Icel. lifa to live, to be left, to remain, Goth. liban to live; akin to E. leave to forsake, and life, Gr. lip to anoint, smear; -- the first sense prob. was, to cleave to, stick to; hence, to remain, stay; and hence, to live.

livelihood.etymology: OE. livelode, liflode, prop., course of life, life's support, maintenance, fr. AS. lif life + lad road, way, maintenance. Confused with livelihood liveliness. See Life, and Lode.

liver.etymology: AS. lifer; akin to D. liver, G. leber, OHG. lebara, Icel. lifr, Sw. lefver, and perh. to Gr. live, v.

livery.etymology: OE. livere, F. livrée, formerly, a gift of clothes made by the master to his servants, prop., a thing delivered, fr. livrer to deliver, L. liberare to set free, in LL., to deliver up. See Liberate.

livid.etymology: L. lividus, from livere to be of a blush color, to be black and blue: cf. F. livide.

lizard.etymology: OE. lesarde, OF. lesarde, F. lézard, L. lacerta, lacertus. Cf. Alligator, Lacerta.

llano.etymology: Sp., plain even, level. See Plain.

load.etymology: OE. lode load, way; properly the same word as lode, but confused with lade, load, v. See Lade, Lead, v., Lode.

loaf.etymology: OE. lof, laf, AS. hlaf; akin to G. laib, OHG. hleip, Icel. hleifr, Goth. hlaifs, Russ. khlieb', Lith. klëpas. Cf. Lady, Lammas, Lord.

loafer.etymology: G. läufer a runner, Prov. G. laufer, lofer, fr. laufen to run. See Leap.

loam.etymology: AS. lam; akin to D. leem, G. lehm, and E. lime. See 4th Lime.

loath.etymology: OE. looth, loth, AS. la hostile, odious; akin to OS. l, G. leid, Icel. lei, Sw. led, G. leiden to suffer, OHG. lidan to suffer, go, cf. AS. li to go, Goth. leipan, and E. lead to guide.

loathe.etymology: AS. la to hate. See Loath.

lob.etymology: W. llob an unwieldy lump, a dull fellow, a blockhead. Cf. Looby, Lubber.

lobby.etymology: LL. lobium, lobia, laubia, a covered portico fit for walking, fr. OHG.louba, G. laube, arbor. See Lodge.

lobelia.etymology: NL. So called from Lobel, botanist to King James I.

lobscouse.etymology: Written also lobscourse from which lobscouse is corrupted.

lobster.etymology: AS. loppestre, lopystre prob., corrupted fr. L. locusta a marine shellfish, a kind of lobster, a locust. Cf. Locust.

lobule.etymology: Cf. F. lobule, dim. of lobe. See Lobe.

local.etymology: L. localis, fr. locus place: cf. F. local. See Lieu, Locus.

locate.etymology: L. locatus, p. p. of locare to place, fr. locus place. See Local.

loch.etymology: Gael. & Olr. loch. See Lake of water.

lock.etymology: AS. loc inclosure, an inclosed place, the fastening of a door, fr. lucan to lock, fasten; akin to OS. lukan (in comp.), D. luiken, OHG. luhhan, Icel. l, Goth. lukan (in comp.); cf. Skr. ruj to break. Cf. Locket.

locket.etymology: F. loquet latch, dim. of OF. loc latch, lock; of German origin. See Lock a fastening.

locomotion.etymology: L. locus place + motio motion: cf. F. locomotion. See Local, and Motion.

locus.etymology: L., place. Cf. Allow, Couch, Lieu, Local.

locust.etymology: L. locusta locust, grasshopper. Cf. Lobster.

locution.etymology: L. locutio, fr. loqui to speak: cf. F. locution.

lode.etymology: AS. lad way, journey, fr. li\'eban to go. See Lead to guide, and cf. Load a burden.

lodge.etymology: OE. loge, logge, F. loge, LL. laubia porch, gallery, fr. OHG. louba, G. laube, arbor, bower, fr. lab foliage. See Leaf, and cf. Lobby, Loggia.

lodgment.etymology: Cf. F. logement. See Lodge, v.

loft.etymology: Icel. lopt air, heaven, loft, upper room; akin to AS. lyft air, G. luft, Dan. loft loft, Goth. luftus air. Cf. Lift, v. & n.

logic.etymology: OE. logike, F. logique, L. logica, logice, Gr. Legend.

roots.meaning: A suffix indicating something drawn or written, a drawing, writing; -- as, monogram, telegram, chronogram.
A combining form signifying impressed form; stamp; print; type; typical form; representative; as in stereotype phototype, ferrotype, monotype.

logwood.etymology: So called from being imported in logs.

loin.etymology: OE. loine, OF. logne, F. longe, from (assumed) LL. lumbea, L. lumbus join. Cf. Lends, Lumbar, Nombles.

loiter.etymology: D. leuteren to delay, loiter; cf; Prov. G. lottern to be louse, lotter louse, slack, unsettled, vagrant, OHG. lotar.

loki.etymology: Icel. Loki, perh. akin to lokka, locka to allure, entice.

loll.etymology: Cf. Icel. lolla to act lazily, loll, lolla, laziness, OD. lollen to sit over the fire, and E. lull. Cf. Lill, Lull.

lollipop.etymology: Perhaps fr. Prov. E. loll to soothe + pope a mixed liquor.

lombard.etymology: F. lombard, fr. the Longobardi or Langobardi, i. e., Longbeards, a people of Northern Germany, west of the Elbe, and afterward in Northern Italy. See Long, and Beard, and cf. Lumber.

loment.etymology: L. lomentum a mixture of bean meal and rice, used as a cosmetic wash, bean meal, fr. lavare, lotum, to wash.

long.etymology: AS. long, lang; akin to OS, OFries., D., & G. lang, Icel. langr, Sw. lång, Dan. lang, Goth. laggs, L.longus. sq. root125. Cf. Length, Ling a fish, Linger, Lunge, Purloin.

longanimity.etymology: L. longanimitas; longus long + animus mind: cf. F. longanimité.

longicorn.etymology: L. longus long + cornu horn: cf. F. longicorne.

longitude.etymology: F., fr. L. longitudo, fr. longus long.

loo.etymology: For older lanterloo, F. lanturelu, lanturlu, name of the game; orig., the refrain of a vaudeville.

look.etymology: OE. loken, AS. locian; akin to G. lugen, OHG. luogen.

loom.etymology: OE. lome, AS. gel utensil, implement.

loon.etymology: Scot. loun, lown, loon; akin to OD. loen a stupid man; prob. for an older lown, and akin to E. lame.

loop.etymology: G. luppe an iron lump. Cf. Looping.

looping.etymology: Cf. D. loopen to run. Cf. Loop a mass of iron, Leap.

loos.etymology: OE. los, fr. OF. los, laus.

loose.etymology: OE. loos, lous, laus, Icel. lauss; akin to OD. loos, D. los, AS. leás false, deceitful, G. los, loose, Dan. & Sw. lös, Goth. laus, and E. lose. Lose, and cf. Leasing falsehood.

loot.etymology: Hind. l, Skr. l, l, booty, lup to break, spoil; prob. akin to E. rob.

lopper.etymology: Cf. Prov. G. lübbern, levern, OHG. giliber, G. luppe, lab, rennet.

lord.etymology: OE. lord, laverd, loverd, AS. hlaford, for hlafweard, i. e., bread keeper; hlaf bread, loaf + weardian to look after, to take care of, to ward. See Loaf, and Ward to guard, and cf. Laird, Lady.

roots.meaning: A suffix forming adjectives and adverbs, and denoting likeness or resemblance.

lorica.etymology: L., lit., a corselet of thongs, fr. lorum thong.

lorry.etymology: Prob. from lurry to pull or lug.

lose.etymology: OE. losien to loose, be lost, lose, AS. losian to become loose; akin to OE. leosen to lose, p. p. loren, lorn, AS. leósan, p. p. loren (in comp.), D. verliezen, G. verlieren, Dan. forlise, Sw. förlisa, förlora, Goth. fraliusan, also to E. loose, a & v., L. luere to loose, Gr. l to cut. sq. root127. Cf. Analysis, Palsy, Solve, Forlorn, Leasing, Loose, Loss.

loss.etymology: AS. los loss, losing, fr. leósan to lose. Lose, v. t.

lost.etymology: Prop. p. p. of OE. losien. See Lose, v. t.

lot.etymology: AS. hlot; akin to hleótan to cast lots, OS. hl lot, D. lot, G. loos, OHG. l, Icel. hlutr, Sw. lott, Dan. lod, Goth. hlauts. Cf. Allot, Lotto, Lottery.

lothario.etymology: Name of a character in Rowe's drama, "The Fair Penitent."

lotion.etymology: L. lotio, fr. lavare, lotum, to wash: cf. F. lotion. See Lave to wash.

lotto.etymology: F. loto or It. lotto, prop., a lot; of German origin. See Lot.

loud.etymology: OE. loud, lud, AS. hl; akin to OS. hl, D. luid, OHG. l, G. laut, L. -clutus, in inclutus, inclitus, celebrated, renowned, cluere to be called, Gr. . Client, Listen, Slave a serf.

lounge.etymology: OE. lungis a tall, slow, awkward fellow, OF. longis, longin, said to be fr. Longinus, the name of the centurion who pierced the body of Christ, but with reference also to L. longus long. Cf. Long, a.

louse.etymology: OE. lous, AS. l, pl. l; akin to D. luis, G. laus, OHG. l, Icel. l, Sw. lus, Dan. luus; perh. so named because it is destructive, and akin to E. lose, loose.

lout.etymology: OE. louten, luten, AS. l; akin to Icel. l, Dan. lude, OHG. l to lie hid.

louver.etymology: OE. lover, OF. lover, lovier; or l'ouvert the opening, fr. overt, ouvert, p. p. of ovrir, ouvrir, to open, F. ouvrir. Cf. Overt.

louvre.etymology: OE. lover, OF. lover, lovier; or l'ouvert the opening, fr. overt, ouvert, p. p. of ovrir, ouvrir, to open, F. ouvrir. Cf. Overt.

lovage.etymology: F. livèche, fr. L. levisticum, ligusticum, a plant indigenous to Liguria, lovage, from Ligusticus Ligustine, Ligurian, Liguria a country of Cisalpine Gaul.

love.etymology: OE. love, luve, AS. lufe, lufu; akin to E.lief, believe, L. lubet, libet,it pleases, Skr. lubh to be lustful. See Lief.

low.etymology: OE. lowen, AS. hl; akin to D. loeijen, OHG. hl, hluojan.

loyal.etymology: F. loyal, OF. loial, leial, L. legalis, fr. lex, legis, law. See Legal, and cf. Leal.

loyalty.etymology: Cf. F. loyaute. See Loyal, and cf. Legality.

lozenge.etymology: F. lozange, losange; perh. the same as OF. losengef flattery, praise, the heraldic sense being the oldest (cf. E. hatchment, blazon). Cf. Losenger, Laudable.

lubber.etymology: Cf. dial. Sw. lubber. See Looby, Lob.

lubricant.etymology: L. lubricans, p. pr. of lubricare, See Lubricate.

lubricate.etymology: L. lubricatus, p. p. of lubricare to lubricate. See Lubric.

luce.etymology: OF. lus, L. lucius a kind of fish.

lucent.etymology: L. lucens, p. pr. of lucere to shine, fr. lux, lucis, light.

lucid.etymology: L. lucidus, fr. lux, lucis, light. See Light, n.

lucifer.etymology: L., bringing light, n., the morning star, fr. lux, lucis, light + ferre to bring.

luck.etymology: Akin to D. luk, geluk, G. glück, Icel. lukka, Sw. lycka, Dan. lykke, and perh. to G. locken to entice. Cf. 3d Gleck.

lucrative.etymology: L. lucrativus, fr. lucrari to gain, fr. lucrum gain: cf. F. lucratif. See Lucre.

lucubrate.etymology: L. lucubratus, p. p. of lucubrare to work by lamplight, fr. lux light. See Light, n.

luculent.etymology: L. luculentus, from lux, lucis, light.

ludicrous.etymology: L. ludicrus, or ludicer, from ludus play, sport, fr. ludere to play.

luff.etymology: OE. lof, prob. a sort of timber by which the course of a ship was directed, perh. a sort of paddle; cf. D. loef luff, loeven to luff. The word is perh. akin to E. glove. Cf. Aloof.

lugubrious.etymology: L. lugubris, fr. lugere to mourn; cf. Gr. ruj to break.

luke.etymology: Prob. fr. lew, perh. influenced by AS. wlæc warm, lukewarm, remiss. Cf. Lew.

lull.etymology: Akin to OD. lullen to sing to sleep, G. lullen, Dan. lulle, Sw. lulla; all of imitative origin. Cf. Loll, Lollard.

lumbago.etymology: L., fr. lumbus loin. See Lumbar.

lumber.etymology: Prob. fr. Lombard, the Lombards being the money lenders and pawnbrokers of the Middle Ages. A lumber room was, according to Trench, originally a Lombard room, or room where the Lombard pawnbroker stored his pledges. See Lombard.

lumen.etymology: L., light, an opening for light.

luminary.etymology: F. luminaire, L. luminare a light or lamp, which was lighted in the churches, a luminary, fr. lumen, luminis, light, fr. lucere to be light, to shine, lux, lucis, light. See Light.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying beginning, beginning to be; as, adolescent, effervescent, etc.

luminous.etymology: L. luminosus, fr. lumen light: cf. F. lumineux. See Luminary, Illuminate.

lump.etymology: Cf. OD. lompe piece, mass. Cf. Lunch.

lumpfish.etymology: From Lump, on account of its bulkiness: cf. G. & D. lump, F. lompe.

luna.etymology: L.; akin to lucere to shine. See Light, n., and cf. Lune.

lunar.etymology: L. lunaris, fr. luna the moon. See Luna, and cf. Lunary.

lunate.etymology: L. lunatus crescent-shaped, p. p. of lunare to bend like a crescent, fr. luna the moon.

lunatic.etymology: F. lunatique, L. lunaticus, fr. luna the moon. See Lunar.

lunch.etymology: Of uncertain etymol. Cf. Prov. Eng. nunc a lump.

luncheon.etymology: Prov. E. luncheon, lunchion, lunshin, a large lump of food, fr. lunch. See Lunch.

lunette.etymology: F., dim. of lune moon, L.luna. See Lune a crescent.

lung.etymology: OE. lunge, AS. lunge, pl. lungen; akin to D. long, G. lunge, Icel. & Sw. lunga, Dan. lunge, all prob. from the root of E. light. See Light not heavy.

lunge.etymology: Also spelt longe, fr. allonge. See Allonge, Long.

lunisolar.etymology: L. luna moon + E. solar: cf. F. lunisolaire.

lunt.etymology: D. lont; akin to Dan. & G. lunte, Sw. lunta. Cf. Link a torch.

lunula.etymology: L., prop., a little moon. See Lunule.

lunule.etymology: F., fr. L. lunula, dim. of luna moon.

lupine.etymology: L. lupinus, lupinum, apparently fr. lupinus belonging to a wolf, fr. lupus a wolf; perh. so called because it was supposed to exhaust the soil: cf. F. lupin. Cf. Wolf.

lure.etymology: OF. loire, loirre, loerre, F. leurre lure, decoy; of German origin; cf. MHG. luoder, G. luder lure, carrion.

lurk.etymology: OE. lurken, lorken, prob. a dim. from the source of E. lower to frown. See Lower, and cf. Lurch, a sudden roll, Lurch to lurk.

luscious.etymology: Prob. for lustious, fr. lusty, or perh. a corruption of luxurious. Cf. Lush, Lusty.

lush.etymology: Prob. an abbrev. of lushious, fr. luscious.

lust.etymology: AS. lust, lust, pleasure, longing; akin to OS., D., G., & Sw. lust, Dan. & Icel. lyst, Goth lustus, and perh. tom Skr. lush to desire, or to E. loose. Cf. List to please, Listless.

lustrate.etymology: L. lustratus, p. p. of lustrare to lustrate, fr. lustrum. See Lustrum.

lusty.etymology: From Lust. See Lust, and cf. Luscious.

lutanist.etymology: LL.lutanista, fr. lutana lute. See Lute the instrument.

lute.etymology: L. lutum mud, clay: cf. OF. lut.

luxate.etymology: L. luxatus, p. p. of luxare to dislocate.

luxuriant.etymology: L. luxurians, p. pr. of luxuriare: cf. F. luxuriant. See Luxuriate.

luxuriate.etymology: L. luxuriatus, p. p. of luxuriari, -are, to luxuriate. See Luxury.

luxurious.etymology: L. luxuriosus: cf. F. luxurieux. See Luxury.

luxury.etymology: L. luxuria, fr. luxus: cf. F. luxure.

lychnis.etymology: L., a kind of red flower, Gr. lychni`s; cf. ly`chnos a lamp.

lye.etymology: AS. leáh; akin to D. loog, OHG. louga, G. lauge; cf. Icel. laug a bath, a hot spring.

roots.meaning: Combining forms of the Greek word for gland; -- used in words relating to the structure, diseases, etc., of the glands.
A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.

lymphatic.etymology: L. lymphaticus distracted, frantic: cf. F. lymphatique

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.
A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.
A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.

lynx.etymology: L. lynx, lyncis, Gr. lox, G. luchs, prob. named from its sharp sight, and akin to E. light. See Light, n., and cf. Ounce an animal.

lyonnaise.etymology: F. lyonnaise, fem. of lyonnais of Lyons.

lyre.etymology: OE. lire, OF. lyre, L. lyra, Gr. Lyra.

lyric.etymology: L. lyricus, Gr. lyrique. See Lyre.

lyrical.etymology: L. lyricus, Gr. lyrique. See Lyre.
